commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring vendors to disclose sensitive and social-determinant inputs, bias assessment methods, and mitigation evidence during procurement changes which tools health systems buy or reduces biased performance after deployment. Ten sources endorse the practice, two at the "must" level, but the support rests on guidance, frameworks, and commentary rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The ten endorsements consist of two frameworks, two guidance documents, and six commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert agreement does not substitute for comparative data, so certainty about the effect of procurement disclosure on purchasing decisions or patient outcomes cannot be rated.

One endorsing source states that, starting in 2025, EHR developers supplying Predictive DSIs must disclose specific attributes and inform users whether demographic, social-determinant, or health assessment data are used. That requirement applies to tools supplied within an EHR offering. Procurement contract terms may be the main route for obtaining similar disclosure from other vendors.

Several endorsing commentaries frame procurement disclosure as an equity safeguard and ask for subgroup performance and dataset representativeness. No study shows whether vendors' disclosed subgroup results reflect performance in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Disclosure of this kind may reveal gaps without closing them.

No study in this set measures how often tools bought without bias information later produce harmful subgroup errors. The size of the hazard this safeguard targets is therefore undocumented here. The CHAI guide's suggestion of third-party bias evaluation implies that endorsers do not regard vendor self-report alone as a sufficient check.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or purchasing cycles with and without structured bias-disclosure requirements. Such studies should measure whether disclosures change which tools are selected, whether disclosed subgroup results match local validation, and whether post-deployment subgroup performance differs. Research should also assess how complete and accurate vendor disclosures are when checked against independent evaluation.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of this practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that vendor-disclosed bias results apply to their patients and may need to request subgroup data matching their own population or run local validation.
